name: Wendy Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead four donation coordinators for a large grocery company. We match surplus food from stores with food banks, schedule vans and check why a chilled box was refused. I moved from store receiving into this junior lead role nine months ago and still ask the food-safety officer about temperature rules. I have a bachelor's degree and use AI every day to draft routes, then call a person to confirm the crates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like when the vans finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and live with Elias, who sells woodworking jobs to paying customers. Our children are grown and live elsewhere. Our flat is paid off, my manager pay is high, and we keep eleven months of expenses in cash; there are plenty of other large retailers nearby. Retirement is in sight, but we have not checked either pension's eligibility date or net monthly amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route helper will still save a few minutes and my four coordinators will still talk to stores and food banks. The paid-off flat and eleven months saved mean our living costs feel secure while I earn this higher wage. I am still learning which food labels the safety officer will accept, so a small tool is about all I want to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell store staff to put the allergen label where the food bank can actually see it. I'd tell our coordinators that a route is finished only when the receiver accepts the food. I'd tell Elias that a mild AI year doesn't change our household budget much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm only nine months into leading this team and make the food-safety officer check my doubtful calls. In a plateau I expect the job to remain, and plenty of nearby retailers have similar teams. Our cash gives me room to get the work right rather than rush a box onto a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This Thursday I'll have the team check the nine donated bakery crates returned for missing labels against the stores' original packing sheets. I'll keep using the existing AI route draft only after a coordinator confirms the destination, and ask the food-safety officer for a written rule on unreadable allergen labels before resending any crate. I won't add a new system to a process we haven't got straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our pay and work. The returned bread is annoying because a family could have eaten it if we had labelled it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the bread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The store wrote the ingredients on a loose card that fell off one crate. The food bank refused all nine crates because it could not tell which loaves contained nuts. Bread with no readable allergen label is not a useful donation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your reserve cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eleven months of food, utilities, health costs and Elias's workshop insurance at our current spending. That does not mean I can spend it on every new machine. Our grown children have their own bills, and we do not count their earnings.

say: I'd tell stores to attach **readable allergen labels** before dispatch.
I'd tell coordinators a route ends when the **food bank accepts** the crates.
think: My new lead job looks **steady** in a modest-change world.
Eleven months cash gives me **time to check** uncertain food-safety calls.
do: Check **nine returned bakery crates** against packing sheets Thursday.
Keep **existing route drafts** under coordinator destination checks.
Ask the **food-safety officer** for a written unreadable-label rule before resending crates.
feel: I feel **calm** about pay while frustrated by wasted bread.

fieldNote: A loose ingredient card made **nine bakery crates** unusable.
She knows her **junior safety limits** despite daily route-tool use.
The existing reserve is **eleven months**, not permission for equipment purchases.

steps.text: Check nine returned bakery crates against original store packing sheets Thursday
Ask food-safety officer for written allergen-label rule before resending crates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing allocations, checking stock, booking vans and answering food banks are the bulk of my desk. Stronger AI can do that quickly, and I can see the company leaving fewer paid coordinators. The people handling crates may have work longer, but my lead job is mostly plans and messages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff association to count every paid coordinator hour that disappears from the proposed rota. I'd tell the food banks who has authority when an allergen label is missing. I'd tell my team I won't call a smaller desk efficient until the receiving records show it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior lead role could be cut if one manager oversees several automated routes. Daily AI use does not give me the qualified officer's job, and the pay here is worth protecting. The paid-off flat and eleven months cash give us choices, but I would still have to replace a high wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in January I'll join the monthly staff-association meeting and bring the actual paid hours for four coordinators to the director's staffing discussion. I'll keep a hand-checked log of allergen-label refusals for the first year and ask the qualified officer to sign off any change to rejection rules before my team uses it. I'll wait for the written staffing plan before applying for another manager post; I won't cut a clerk's shift myself on a software forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for my own post as well as the four people I lead. Cash gives us time, but it doesn't replace an evening wage for a clerk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring hours instead of case counts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The proposal counts faster routes but not the paid evening calls when a food bank refuses a crate. A shorter rota cannot read an allergy label for a family. I want the director to see both the hours and the failed deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let AI decide a rejection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It may be better than I am at reading labels in this picture, but the company still needs a clear rule for appeals. The safety officer owns that rule, not me. I would keep existing checks until the officer signs a new procedure.

I'd tell food banks the **qualified officer** decides missing-label appeals.

Eleven months cash helps, but **high pay** would still need replacing.

Keep a **hand-checked refusal log** through the first year; change checks only after the safety officer signs a procedure.
Wait for the **written staffing plan** before applying for another manager post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could plan the routes, read the labels and answer food banks better and cheaper than our desk. I think my junior lead post is likely to end, and nearby planning offices would face the same thinking change. People still move crates until capable robots arrive around 2031, while their bookings change in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the coordinators to ask for the date and terms of any paid-hour cut in writing. I'd tell the food banks to keep a record of refused crates so an AGI decision can be challenged. I'd tell Elias that a paid-off home buys time, not an excuse to guess at retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the lead wage to go, though I cannot know whether a company keeps a few human contacts. With eleven months cash and a paid-off flat we can search without an immediate utility crisis; Elias's net woodworking sales would not replace my higher pay by themselves. I would worry about the years before an actual pension, not about next week's groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask human resources for written notice and severance dates, then request both pension providers' eligibility dates and monthly net estimates. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I'll apply for posted local paid work only after checking duties and wages, accepting only a signed offer whose pay with Elias's confirmed net receipts covers food, utilities, health costs and workshop insurance. I'll keep the eleven-month reserve for the search and volunteer one Saturday at the food bank only if household essentials remain covered; I won't count that shift as pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a high wage, but I can compare offers without panic. I want the pension dates in writing before using the word retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a food-bank warehouse role be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lifting crates is physical until robots around 2031, but the allocation and stock records face AGI in 2028. I don't have a posted warehouse offer or a safe-lifting assessment. Volunteering is not a wage and I won't turn it into one in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Elias expand the workshop instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid orders after material costs show more work than he can already do; we have not established that. I would not buy a machine from emergency cash to chase a guess. His sales are his, and we plan with net receipts that arrived.

A workshop purchase lacks **extra net orders** and is not in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us a chance to protect wages and make a rule for automated food refusals before my planning desk faces AGI in 2031. Store staff still lift crates until capable robots arrive around 2034, but stock decisions and route orders change in 2031. I cannot claim a physical job without a posting or safe-duty check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell food banks I will ask for a public appeal rule for automatic allergen refusals. I'd tell our staff association about any paid-hour changes. I'd tell Elias we can save from wages now while the flat needs no mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep earning in planning until 2031, but the junior desk could still end. Our paid-off flat and cash reserve give me room to push a rule without putting food on credit. I do not know when our pensions are eligible or what they pay, so I would keep paid work in view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the food-safety officer for permission to use anonymised records of the nine refused bakery crates, then send the regulator a written request for a clear appeal rule for automatic allergen refusals. I'd add 320 monthly to cash only while my wage and Elias's confirmed net sales cover food, utilities, health costs and workshop insurance, pausing if his paid orders fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my desk ends I'd apply for posted local work with wages that, alongside his net receipts, cover those costs; I would leave this post only for a signed offer if it remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a desk loss, though five years lets me work on the rule and our cash. A public rule would help food banks even if it never saves my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you send the crate records yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without the officer's permission and removing the store and customer names. I can describe the problem from public information if permission is refused. An appeal rule needs evidence, not someone's private shopping list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Elias has a quiet month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 320 extra transfer stops before it eats our eleven-month reserve. We pay ordinary costs from confirmed income and recheck the budget. I won't call a quoted woodworking job paid until the customer pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be sixty-eight in 2036, and our grown children will still have their own homes. My donation planning desk faces AGI then, while capable robots can lift and sort crates around 2039. I cannot tell you our pension eligibility from our ages alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell food banks where to challenge a refused chilled load. I'd tell Elias we should get the flat's energy costs and pension figures into one household budget. I'd tell the coordinators I will not promise a position that the company has not posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade might let me reduce living costs in the paid-off flat while I still earn a higher wage. I expect my junior lead role to be exposed in 2036 even if I use AI every day. I do not know the eligible pension amounts, so I might need paid work after sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll get two written insulation quotes for the flat and the current utility bills; I'd hire an installer only if a safe written plan can be paid from wages without touching eleven months cash and the savings on real bills justify the cost. I'd request both pension providers' actual eligibility and net monthly amounts, then compare the combined figure with Elias's confirmed net receipts and our food, utility, health and insurance costs. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stop paid work only if those eligible incomes cover essentials; otherwise I'd apply for posted local paid work with hours and wages that cover the shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about an uncertain wage and pension, though the flat gives us room to choose. I don't want a birthday to be the only number in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would insulation guarantee lower bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd compare the written price with our actual heating use and have the installer explain what can be done safely. A lower bill on a brochure is not a lower bill at our table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children take you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have homes of their own, and neither has offered that. Elias and I would not count a child's spare room or wages in this plan. We can ask about a one-off emergency if needed and respect the answer.

Apply if pension plus Elias's net receipts fall short; require workable hours and adequate wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a planning desk can disappear before our food-bank partners and coordinators have an appeal or wage plan. Written severance dates, actual pension eligibility and a real posted paid job would help. Our paid-off flat and eleven months cash give us time to ask, while Elias's net sales alone do not replace my wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the family who did not receive the donated bread whether a shorter route mattered. The allergen card fell off before the van reached the food bank. Food on a map is not food on a table.

headlineQuote: Food on a map is not food on a table.
portrait: Wendy, **58**, recently became junior lead of four grocery donation coordinators after years in store receiving.
She uses AI **daily** for routes, while the food-safety officer checks allergen rules she is still learning.
Her higher wage, paid-off flat and **eleven months cash** support her and Elias, whose woodworking sales vary.
She presses for paid-hour records and **appeal rules**, then judges retirement against actual pensions and net household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her planning wage before staff and food banks have a clear appeal and pay plan.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written severance dates** and a clear route to challenge automatic food refusals.
She needs **actual pension eligibility** and a posted paid job with enough household income.
